utterances.text: Okay. So just that in this -- in this three days there were special -- a special situation. And special situations, they changed the normal -- the normal things.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And how do you know that, Mr. Hutsch, what's your -- the basis for that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's -- first that what I saw the time in Macedonia, for example, if you were going to the -- to the Aracinovo time, in Aracinovo time the police forces they have been all the time the same when the operation against Aracinovo was going on. If you are going to Tetovo time, for example, there were a check-point in front of the football stadium in Tetovo, and especially when we have had an incident where an Albanian-thrown hand-grenade to this check-point, and by the name Mattias Rub, your favourite journalist, he wrote that was just a mobile phone but never the mind when this incident happened. For example, the police forces there have been also been there for more than 12 hours and 20 hours and 24 hours. I spoke to policemen who worked for 48 hours and 72 hours without a minute of sleep.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, would you agree that at least as far as Mr. Georgievski is concerned, he says that this system was applicable in August of 2001. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a normal system, but he wasn't asked if that was the system on the 10th, 11th and 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, on the 24th of May of 2007, there's a witness who appeared in this case, and he was asked the following question about shifts: "Is it correct that the shifts took place at every 12 hours?" That's the question. "Yes." And then the answer is: "In the morning you would drive your colleagues to the check-points where they were deployed and, at the same time you would bring the previous shift back. Is that correct?" "Yes." And then there's a further question: "Because of the situation that we discussed just now, sometimes it wasn't possible simply to have a sufficient number of regular police officers for all of the check-points or sometimes only reserve police officers would be at the check-points at a given time. Is that correct?" "I said previously that the number of regular police officers was insufficient for such purposes. So the reserve police officer assisted." Again you would agree, sir, that this person who is M-083, did not suggest that at the time there was any other shift system that was applicable in the area. Do you agree with that? He did not make that suggestion.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: What he said is not exactly to the situation that we have had between the 10th and 12th. And for example we have had check-point in the entrance of the Erebino mountain, and sometimes this check-point, there was nobody in. They have just some sand sacks there, and during the trebos crisis, this check-point was -- was -- there have been policemen 24 hours. The same if you was going to the highway from Skopje to Tetovo, there have been check-points there, they even didn't control in normal times the cars on this highway. But they did so when something happened, for example, in Tetovo, or something happened at Gobcin [phoen], for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: So we are talking about the normal things, but the situation wasn't normal in Ljuboten area between the 11th and -- between the 10th and the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But in fact this is another element which shows that your story is false, isn't that correct, Mr. Hutsch?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which element?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: The fact that you could not have met the same persons on two different occasions at the time and places where you said you met them. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where are the different occasions?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, one is 1530 on the 11th of August and the other one is 7.20 on the morning of the 12th, as you agreed a moment ago. So do you agree that if the evidence of these two persons, M-083 and Mr. Georgievski are to be believed and in fact, as the evidence suggests, there was no change in the month of August to the normal pattern of shifts, you could not have met those same people at what you say was a check-point. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why not? Because if they set up this check-point at 6.00 and they leave at 6.00 in the evening, they are there for 12 hours. And next morning, they have 12 hours rest and return and next morning at 6.00 and they stay there until 6.00 in the evening, so where is my wide spread? I don't understand what are you discussing.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, what I'm discussing, sir, is that the fact that if the shifts pattern that was described by these two individuals is applied, the same person could not be at the same place, do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because they were 12 hours working between 6.00 in the morning and 6.00 in the evening. Then they have 12 hours rest between 6.00 in the evening and 6.00 in the morning, and 6.00 in the morning they start to work again until 6.00 in the evening. Mr. Mettraux, I don't know your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, see, sir, if Mr. Georgievski were to say, for instance, that the shift start started not at 6.00, as you said, but that they started much earlier, that would make it impossible. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, now you are doing that what you are ask -- what you are -- the complete say -- time saying that I'm doing. You are just fixing the -- the -- your testimonies like you need it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, what about -- do you know at what time the shifts were organised at the time during -- in that area during at this particular time?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that earlier you had also mentioned in your statement, and I have read it out to you, that on the 12th of August, the Sunday, you obtained your information at 6.03 and 7.11 from the duty book at the check-point. Do you recall saying that? That's paragraph 61.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: This is another one of those element that gives your story away. Isn't that the case, Mr. Hutsch, there was no such log-book. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think we discussed this matter now.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I will show you paragraph 8 again of Mr. Georgievski's statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Paragraph 7, I apologise. This is Rule 65 ter 1D313. This would be the previous page, please. Thank you. And if we can focus, please, on the last paragraph on that page. Thank you. It says this: "Asked by the Defence and with regards to the check-points in Macedonia during the time of the crisis, I can say that I have passed through check-points on many occasion during the period. I have never seen a log-book on daily events or any kind of register on any of those check-points. I have never heard of anything like that, and as far as I can say from that fact I have also lived in Macedonia during that period as well as while working as a police officer. Such registers or log-book did not exist."

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And that's the situation, Mr. Hutsch, isn't it, that there was no check-point and no log-books to get information from. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree, because your witness himself said there was a police presence in the street between Radisani and Ljubanci. They have had notices. I tried to explain to you with my limited English versions that if -- if it is a official log-book, if is a duty book, or if just private notices, I don't know. Your own witness said if -- if you look to paragraph A -- 8, that he thinks that they had shift system too. That means he is not sure that it was shift 2. But are you presenting all these things like facts to the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But wouldn't you agree, sir, that you invented this story of the log-book to make it more credible that you had obtained information about events that happened earlier this morning. Do you agree that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir, I don't agree because they have had notices. If private or official, I don't know, but they have had notices.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you agree that those two times which you mention, which are 6.03 and 7.11 on the morning of the 12th are times at which you say a number of mortars were fired from the army position into the village or in the direction of the village. Do you agree with that? And I can show you your statement, if you want.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mettraux, I never agreed with something what you said, and so I would like that you don't say "and do you agree," that means I have had agreed to you a lot of times, and still this moment I didn't agree one time. So the next time is -- so why? Why I need these two information for my story, that I was trying to investigate if at 6.03 or 7.11 some mortars were fired into Ljuboten, nobody in Germany was interested in -- even in Macedonia. Nobody was interested in this information, and I got it from the policemen, and that's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And those two times, to answer my question, Mr. Hutsch, were, according to you, times at which mortar fire was fired by the army into the direction of the village. Do you agree with that? And I can show you your statement, if you want.

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: First, Mr. Mettraux, I never agreed with something what you said, and so I would like that you don't say "and do you agree." That means I have had agreed to you a lot of times and still this moment I didn't agree one time. So the next time is -- so why? Why I need these two information for my story, that I was trying to investigate if at 6.03 or 7.11 some mortars were fired into Ljuboten, nobody in Germany was interested in, even in Macedonia, nobody was interested in this information and I got it from the policemen and that's what I wrote.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And those two times, to answer my question, Mr. Hutsch, were, according to you, times at which mortar fire was fired by the army into the village or in the direction of the village of Ljuboten. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I suppose, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that during the --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Otherwise -- otherwise, the mortar teams would have changed between 7.00 and 8.00. That means before 8.00 or before 7.12 other people would have fired the mortars then afterwards. And like I said as well in my examination by Mr. Saxon, that I got the information that the mortar positions were run with army teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: And I got this information but not with my own eyes, and I never said that I saw the mortar teams with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, no. You made that quite clear, Mr. Hutsch, in your statement, and I will show it to you so that you can see what was said exactly. It's Rule 65 ter 1D234 and that's at page 1D00-2576. And if we can look at the top of the page, please, paragraph 59 and 60. You will agree that the references as to two times 6.03 hours which refers to 120-millimetre rounds being fired by the army into the direction of the village and 7.11, a second round of three mortar rounds fired from armed position into the village. Is that correct, is that's what those paragraphs say?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. But in the very first beginning of my testimony Mr. Saxon asked me how I was knowing who was which unit and which unit was placed where, and I told him that this information was given by a source into the army. So if I'm saying here now that these rounds are fired by the ARM, then it's that what I supposed. Probably they might have been also fired by police forces. Probably they might have been fired by civilians. Whoever else?

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Are you saying now that you got that information from a source in the army, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that not now. I'm saying that in the beginning of my testimony, that the information Mr. Saxon asked me several times and we painted that where the positions of the army and the position of the police have been and I told him this -- in this -- on this background that the information that there was army positions there, that I got this information by -- by army sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if you look at paragraph 61, in fact it suggests that you got that information from the police officers at the check-point. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: The information that the mortars have been fired. But they didn't tell me that was Saso Georgievski who was firing the mortar.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And are you saying, Mr. Hutsch -- do you remember -- let me ask you that way. You remember being asked about those two times during the examination in chief and I objected to the fact that you had your records or binder open before you. Do you recall that? It was on the 26th of June of 2007, and you closed it. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember if I have had the binder in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, is it correct that when you were asked about those times without the benefit of your statement, which is normal, you could not exactly remember these two times as precisely as they are stated in this statement. Do you recall that? You could remember that they were around 6.00 and 7.11?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But you agree that four years after the events when you gave that statement, that's August of 2005, almost four years to the day from the events, you were able to give a record to the minute to the Office of the Prosecutor, 6.03, 7.11. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because I have had my notices with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, if you can be shown what is exhibit P308, Mr. Hutsch. This would be tab 30, exhibit P308. And again, Mr. Hutsch, this is your note, but this time the note of the 12th of August of 2001. And I'll ask the registry, please, to turn to the first -- the first page or the second page, I apologise, in the English, please, and in the German. Do you see, Mr. Hutsch, that is the first page or the first annotation that you made on the 12th of August in your book and the first annotation on that day is at 7.48. Do you see that? And it refers to a telephone with Mr. Beqiri. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And you would agree that there is no references anywhere to the two incidents, the 6.03 and the 7.11 which were given to you as information from either or or and the army and members of the police?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was another exhibit that was my map that I was drawing there, and I tried with my limited English words, and obviously you didn't understand, that there was a combination of writing these notices and drawing this map, and if you would be fair, you would show now the map and there you will see these two informations.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But do you agree that as far as your note are concerned, you did not mention any such events which you recall in your statement?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, because that is not the truth. There is a combination between the map and this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Did you ever verify this information, Mr. Hutsch, which you gave to the Prosecution about your -- the information which you say you obtained about fires -- mortars having been fired at the village at 6.03 and 7.11? Did you make any effort to verify that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And in fact the information is that there was no mortar fire at that time. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, because I didn't check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: There's another matter which I would like to turn to and it relates to your notes. Perhaps, we have three more minutes, I can ask you those general questions. You've indicated to the Office of the Prosecutor when you started your evidence that you would keep work notes as part of your work and I think you've indicated that you would do so on a daily basis. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And as far as can you recall, did you keep any notes for the other days, the 10 and 11 of August of 2001?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't do that in -- in this way.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So what you saying is that you only kept notes for the 12th and the 14th of August, as far as the events of Ljuboten is concerned? Is that your evidence?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was just asked to hand over the notebooks from the 12th and from the 14th, because there are other things in the -- in my notices from the 10th and from the 11th.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: So what you're saying, so I understand you properly is that although notes exist of what you did on the 10th and 11th, they contain material which does not relate to Ljuboten and this explained why you have not provided those to the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, would you agree, sir, that on -- in March or late March or early April of 2007, the Prosecution, on behalf of the Defence, asked you to disclose your notes that covered the period 5 to 24th of August of 2001. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And do you recall that you declined to do so?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I'll show you then what is Rule 65 ter 1D23. First let me show you the request. It's Rule 65 ter 236, please. It's 1D00-2655. Mr. Hutsch, what I'm about to show you is a letter sent by the Defence of Mr. Boskoski to the Office of the Prosecution. I'm grateful. If the registry could focus on the bottom of the page, please. This is what the Defence wrote to the Prosecution: "In his statement of 25th to 27th August of 2005 at paragraph 14 Mr. Hutsch claims to have, 'normally used one notebook per day to take notes of his activities during that time.' The Defence has been provided with records of notebooks of 12 and 14 August. The Defence respectfully asks you to request Mr. Hutsch to provide you with his notebooks from the period 5 August to 24 August. We would in turn ask to you disclose those immediately to the Defence." Do you recall the Prosecution passing on this request to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was I think one of the questions Mr. Kuehnel gave to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: And can you recall what at that time you told Mr. Kuehnel?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't remember what I gave as a answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: But is it correct that you declined to provide those notes to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because -- there were -- there were -- that means you are asking from the 5th up to the 24th of August. For example, on the 10th of August, I have had other investigations and on the 5th of August I have had other --

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Well, but what you told --

utterances.speaker: FRANZ-JOSEF HUTSCH [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just made a break to let you work. I have had a number of other investigations and research in Macedonia where sources are in and all these things. So what you would like to have is the complete archive of 19 days of a journalist with all sources with all their things, and you can't really imagine that I would hand over these notebooks to the -- to the -- to the Defence or even to somebody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Could we please see Rule 65 ter 1D238.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think not, Mr. Mettraux.

utterances.speaker: MR. METTRAUX
utterances.text: Caught by the clock.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Two minutes over time here. I thought you were just going to finish a point. We must adjourn for the day. I'm sure that both you and Mr. Hutsch will welcome a rest. You're each having to work with English. We're grateful. We resume tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 16th day of October, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 7.00 p.m.,
